name: Groove as Motor Prediction Optimization
short_description: Groove — the pleasurable urge to move to music — is the motor prediction system operating in its optimal zone: temporal predictions are strong but rhythmic complexity produces moderate prediction errors
higher_order_principle: Groove instantiates the universal Goldilocks principle in the rhythmic domain. Low syncopation (metronome) = no groove (too predictable). High syncopation (random) = no groove (beat lost). Moderate syncopation = maximal groove (motor system in optimal prediction zone). The same inverted-U function operates in visual complexity (architecture), harmonic surprise (music-pitch), and desirable difficulty (education).

neural_substrate.basal_ganglia: Beat extraction — maximal activation at moderate syncopation

goldilocks_function.low_syncopation: Low groove — rhythm too predictable, no motor engagement
goldilocks_function.high_syncopation: Low groove — beat lost, motor system disengages
goldilocks_function.neural_switch: High syncopation activates cerebellar/prefrontal (interval-timing) instead of BG (beat-based)

causal_links.evidence_base: Witek et al. (2014, ~400 citations): definitive study showing inverted-U between syncopation and groove ratings. Replicated in Witek et al. (2017).
BG-motor loop activation correlates with groove ratings; dopaminergic reward from temporal prediction likely mediates pleasure.

scope_conditions: Applies to rhythmic music with beat structure
Groove requires beat presence — random rhythms cannot produce groove
The Goldilocks zone (~30-50% syncopation) is approximate and may vary by style
moderators: Musical training may shift the Goldilocks zone toward higher complexity
Cultural familiarity with rhythmic vocabulary affects syncopation tolerance

interactions.nature: T2 visual Goldilocks and M9 rhythmic Goldilocks are the same principle in different domains
M8 oscillators provide the mechanism; M9 specifies the optimal operating zone

key_references.citation: Witek, M. A. G., Clarke, E. F., Wallentin, M., Kringelbach, M. L., & Vuust, P. (2014). Syncopation, body-movement and pleasure in groove music. PLoS ONE, 9(4), e94446.
Witek, M. A. G., et al. (2017). Syncopation affects free body-movement in musical groove. Experimental Brain Research, 235(4), 995-1005.
Janata, P., Tomic, S. T., & Haberman, J. M. (2012). Sensorimotor coupling in music and the psychology of the groove. Journal of Experimental Psychology: General, 141(1), 54-75.
